body:
Three levels of the SDG framework

The SDG framework contains different levels of commitment and measurement. A goal states a broad development objective. A target identifies a more specific result to be achieved. An indicator provides a defined measure for tracking progress towards a target.

These terms are related but cannot be used interchangeably.

Example: SDG 6

Goal 6 is Clean Water and Sanitation. Its overall concern is ensuring the availability and sustainable management of water and sanitation for all.

Target 6.1 calls for universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water for all by 2030.

Indicator 6.1.1 measures the proportion of the population using safely managed drinking water services.

Thus, a goal is the broad objective, a target identifies what is to be achieved, and an indicator measures an aspect of achievement.

Why an indicator needs a precise definition

For the international drinking-water indicator, a safely managed service must use an improved source that is located on the premises, available when needed and free from faecal and priority chemical contamination.

Consequently, the existence of a household tap connection does not automatically prove that the household uses a safely managed drinking-water service. Reliability, accessibility and water quality also matter.

Indicators therefore require agreed definitions, appropriate data sources and a clear measurement period. Without these, figures from different locations or years may not be comparable.

Target numbers and indicator numbers

SDG targets and indicators follow a numbering system. Target 6.4 belongs to Goal 6. Indicators 6.4.1 and 6.4.2 are measures connected with that target.

Under Target 6.4:

  • Indicator 6.4.1 measures change in water-use efficiency over time.
  • Indicator 6.4.2 measures water stress through freshwater withdrawal as a proportion of available freshwater resources.

The first indicator concerns efficiency; the second concerns pressure on available freshwater. They measure different aspects of sustainable water management.

Some targets use lettered designations, such as 6.a and 6.b. These commonly concern means of implementation, such as international cooperation, capacity-building or community participation.

The overall Agenda has a 2030 horizon, but not every individual target has a 2030 deadline. For example, Target 6.6 originally specified 2020 for protecting and restoring water-related ecosystems.

What makes the SDGs integrated?

The SDGs are described as integrated and indivisible because progress or failure in one area can influence outcomes in others.

Positive interlinkages

Reliable drinking water can reduce exposure to water-related diseases, contributing to SDG 3 on health. Better access to water may reduce the time households spend collecting it, creating additional opportunities for education and paid work. Efficient agricultural water use can support food security under SDG 2 while reducing pressure on freshwater resources under SDG 6.

Trade-offs and competing demands

Progress towards one objective can also create pressure on another. Expanding irrigation may increase food production but also increase groundwater extraction and electricity demand. Industrial growth may create employment while increasing pollution if environmental safeguards are inadequate.

Such effects are called trade-offs when achieving one objective makes another objective harder to achieve. A well-designed policy attempts to reduce unnecessary trade-offs and strengthen mutually beneficial outcomes.

Data, disaggregation and interpretation

Monitoring should examine both the overall result and how that result is distributed. A rise in the percentage of households with safe drinking water may conceal continued shortages among remote villages, poorer households or particular population groups.

Disaggregated data separates observations by relevant characteristics such as location, sex, age, disability or income group, where appropriate and feasible. It helps identify inequalities that are hidden by overall averages.

The global indicator framework was developed through the Inter-Agency and Expert Group on SDG Indicators and adopted by the UN General Assembly through Resolution 71/313 in 2017. It provides a common basis for international monitoring. Countries may also develop national and subnational indicators suited to their circumstances.

An indicator should not be mistaken for the entire goal. One indicator may measure a particular outcome without capturing every aspect of service quality, equity or environmental sustainability.

Prelims focus

  • A goal is broad, a target specifies an intended result and an indicator measures progress.
  • SDG 6 is Clean Water and Sanitation.
  • Target 6.1 concerns universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water by 2030.
  • Indicator 6.1.1 measures the proportion of people using safely managed drinking water services.
  • Indicator 6.4.1 concerns water-use efficiency; Indicator 6.4.2 concerns water stress.
  • Trap: A household tap connection alone does not establish that drinking-water services meet the safely managed definition.

[United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs, SDG 6, Targets 6.1, 6.4 and 6.6 and their global indicators, consulted 1 November 2026; UN-Water, SDG Indicator 6.1.1, definition of safely managed drinking water services, consulted 1 November 2026; United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 71/313 (2017), global indicator framework; United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 70/1 (2015), Preamble and paragraphs 55–59; United Nations Statistics Division, The Sustainable Development Goals Report 2026, Note to the Reader, global indicator framework and data sources.]

title: SDG Goals, Targets, Indicators and Their Interlinkages

body:
Why global goals require local implementation

The Sustainable Development Goals are global in scope, but most practical outcomes are achieved through decisions made within countries, states, districts, cities and villages.

SDG localization means adapting the global goals and targets to local development priorities, institutions, plans, budgets and monitoring systems without losing their underlying purpose.

For example, Goal 6 concerns water and sanitation worldwide. Its local implementation may involve improving drinking-water quality in a village, reducing leakages in a municipality, protecting an aquifer or providing reliable sanitation in an underserved settlement.

The activities differ because local conditions differ, but each can contribute to the same broad global goal.

India's principal institutions

India uses both national and subnational mechanisms to coordinate SDG implementation and monitor progress.

NITI Aayog

NITI Aayog plays a central coordinating and monitoring role in India's SDG framework. It works with states and Union Territories to promote adoption of the goals, strengthen monitoring, identify good practices and encourage cooperation.

The SDG India Index is one of its monitoring tools. The Index compares the performance of states and Union Territories using selected indicators and goal-wise scores.

Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation

The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, or MoSPI, develops and maintains India's National Indicator Framework, or NIF, in consultation with relevant institutions.

The NIF is used to monitor national progress through defined statistical indicators. It is not the same as the more selective indicator set used to construct the SDG India Index.

Different indicator counts refer to different frameworks

In its publication released on 29 June 2026, MoSPI stated that the National Indicator Framework 2026 contained 277 indicators covering all 17 SDGs. This count refers to the national framework in that publication.

By comparison, the SDG India Index 2023–24, released by NITI Aayog on 12 July 2024, used 113 indicators to assess states and Union Territories. It calculated goal-wise scores for 16 SDGs, with Goal 14 excluded from the composite-score calculation because it principally concerns coastal states.

The Index reported an all-India composite score of 71 for 2023–24, compared with 66 in 2020–21 and 57 in its 2018 baseline edition.

The figures 277 and 113 refer to different indicator sets from different publications and years. They should not be treated as contradictory. Likewise, a composite Index score of 71 is a result under that Index's scoring method; it does not mean that India has completed 71% of every SDG target.

State, district and local responsibilities

States and Union Territories can develop State Indicator Frameworks suited to their priorities. District-level monitoring can use District Indicator Frameworks to identify local differences in access to services and development outcomes.

Local implementation commonly involves several connected activities:

  1. Identify local needs and gaps using reliable data and consultation.
  2. Connect those needs to relevant SDG targets and national or state priorities.
  3. Prepare plans, assign responsibilities and mobilize resources.
  4. Implement services or development projects through the appropriate departments and local bodies.
  5. Monitor results, identify excluded groups and revise actions where necessary.

Gujarat's connection with SDG localization

Gujarat provides a direct example of subnational SDG monitoring. NITI Aayog's The Indian Model of SDG Localisation, published in 2022, documented a state-level review system involving a State Empowered Committee and district-level review through District SDG Committees.

The report also documented State and District Indicator Frameworks and an online monitoring tool known as G-SWIFT, short for Gujarat State-Wide Indicators Framework Tool. It described this tool as supporting the tracking of SDG indicators at the district level.

These details describe arrangements recorded in the 2021–22 reporting period; institutional mechanisms and dashboards may subsequently be revised.

A Gujarat water-management example

Consider a district in Gujarat facing seasonal water scarcity. A localized sustainable-development plan could combine improvements in drinking-water supply, rainwater harvesting, efficient agricultural water use and groundwater protection.

The plan would need to distinguish activities from results. Building a water-supply facility is an activity. Reliable delivery of safe drinking water to households is an outcome. Sustained water availability and fair access are additional questions that monitoring should address.

The same approach can help a district administration assess whether progress reaches remote settlements and disadvantaged groups instead of relying solely on district-wide averages.

Why participation matters

Local knowledge can identify problems that aggregated statistics overlook. Residents may know that a water source is seasonal, a school is difficult to reach during monsoon months or a settlement has inadequate drainage.

Participation by communities, local bodies, civil society and other stakeholders can therefore improve the selection of priorities and the monitoring of actual service delivery.

Prelims focus

  • NITI Aayog coordinates and monitors SDG adoption in India and works with states and Union Territories.
  • MoSPI develops India's National Indicator Framework.
  • The National Indicator Framework 2026 contained 277 national SDG indicators.
  • The SDG India Index 2023–24 used 113 indicators and reported an all-India composite score of 71.
  • NITI Aayog's 2022 localization report documented Gujarat's G-SWIFT monitoring tool.
  • Trap: National Indicator Framework counts must not be confused with the indicator count used in a particular edition of the SDG India Index.

[NITI Aayog, The Indian Model of SDG Localisation (2022), Chapter 3, discussion of monitoring frameworks and Gujarat's state profile, reflecting the 2021–22 reporting period; NITI Aayog, SDG India Index 2023–24, release dated 12 July 2024, methodology and composite scores; Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation, Sustainable Development Goals: National Indicator Framework Progress Report, 2026, release dated 29 June 2026; Government of India, Press Information Bureau, releases dated 12 July 2024 and 29 June 2026; United Nations General Assembly, Resolution 70/1 (2015), paragraphs 72–74, consulted 1 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Local participation helps communities identify development priorities and monitor whether services reach everyone.

title: Localizing Sustainable Development Goals in India and Gujarat
